questions.title: Where is it computed?
questions.answer: In Qwen3-4B, a subgraph across layers 17–35. Attention at L24 is flagged by all four non-probing methods, and MLP effects concentrate at L31–35.

questions.title: What form does the horizon take?
questions.answer: Ordered clusters from seconds to centuries, on a curved manifold.

questions.title: When does it become a preference signal?
questions.answer: The horizon direction is unstable across prompt positions until the user-to-assistant boundary, where attention collapses it into a binary signal.

questions.title: Does a stated deadline reach the output?
questions.answer: Not reliably. When only the sooner option can pay out by the deadline, Qwen3-4B outputs select the undeliverable long-term option 47–53% of the time.

questions.title: Does changing the signal change the output?
questions.answer: Yes, in the settings tested. At L44 of Qwen3-32B, long-term outputs move from 33.7% at steering strength −128 to 76.8% unsteered to 93.1% at +128. In Qwen3-4B, steering at L22 gives about 3.4× odds.
questions.strength: Controlled in Qwen3-32B, suggestive in Qwen3-4B

questions.title: Is it really about time?
questions.answer: Not established. Chain reliability is decodable at about 95% in the same subgraph, and the Qwen3-32B direction may also carry abstraction, urgency and framing.

questions.title: How far does this generalize?
questions.answer: Unknown beyond two Qwen3 models. A direction transferred to a monetary task in Qwen3-32B, but both papers test one model family in thinking-disabled settings.

claims.question: where
claims.claim: Four preference-localization methods converge on one subgraph.
claims.dataset: 500 explicit and 500 implicit pairs, plus 4,588 parametric prompts
claims.method: Probing, contrastive attribution, parametric attribution and parametric patching
claims.caveat: Subgraph-level result on a single financial task. A separate classification pipeline surfaces an MLP cluster at L8–L11.

claims.question: where
claims.claim: Activation patching ranks four components above the rest.
claims.value: L24 and L21 attention; L35 and L31 MLPs
claims.method: Parametric activation patching, ranked by mean causal effect
claims.caveat: Finer-grained circuit tracing has not been done.

claims.question: shape
claims.claim: Time horizons form ordered clusters on a curved manifold.
claims.dataset: 4,588 investment choice prompts with optional horizons
claims.method: PCA inside the localized subgraph
claims.caveat: Shown with PCA projections. The main text reports no quantitative separation metric.

claims.question: when
claims.claim: Attention collapses the horizon representation into a binary preference signal at the turn boundary.
claims.dataset: 4,588 investment choice prompts with optional horizons
claims.method: Layer-31 PCA at four turn-transition tokens
claims.caveat: Separation is shown visually. No-horizon samples align with the manifold by the assistant token.

claims.question: deadline
claims.claim: With a deadline only the sooner option can meet, outputs still select the undeliverable long-term option about half the time.
claims.method: Investment-coherence questionnaire
claims.caveat: Single financial task.

claims.question: deadline
claims.claim: Among 30 models on the same instrument, only frontier API models reach high coherence.
claims.model: Claude family, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini, o3
claims.method: Investment-coherence questionnaire
claims.caveat: The paper reports that smaller Claude variants reach this through a binary heuristic that collapses at longer horizons.

claims.question: deadline
claims.claim: Fitted discount rates sit well below human controls.
claims.method: Fitted discount rate k: below 0.005 for the models, about 0.013 for human controls
claims.caveat: The paper reports that these preferences are unstable across contexts.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Steering at L44 widens the gap in long-term outputs between the strongest negative and positive settings.
claims.method: CAA at L44, greedy decoding: 33.7% at −128, 76.8% at 0, 93.1% at +128
claims.caveat: A matched random direction moves choices by at most 5.6 points. |α| = 128 is 36–63% of the unsteered residual norm, a deliberately large perturbation. No prompting baseline is reported.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Sampled decoding preserves the steering pattern.
claims.method: CAA at L44, temperature 0.8, five samples per prompt, at −128, 0 and +128
claims.caveat: Two-sigma standard errors are between 1.8 and 1.9 points.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: The same direction moves outputs on implicit prompts by less.
claims.method: CAA at L44, greedy decoding
claims.caveat: A matched random direction moves choices by at most 5.5 points.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Steering shifts forced-choice scores in both directions.
claims.method: CAA at L22, α = 50: score 0.17 to 1.39, a lift of +1.22
claims.caveat: The abstract calls this suggestive evidence. L21 reaches the same score, and output quality degrades at |α| = 60.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Open-ended outputs shift in the steered direction on an LLM-judged scale.
claims.dataset: Open-ended neutral prompts, scored from −10 to +10
claims.method: CAA at L19–23 and L26, α up to 50, scored by Claude Sonnet 4.6
claims.caveat: The judge is not validated against human ratings. The paper treats these scores as a proxy for direction, not a calibrated measure.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Moderate long-term steering raises a planning-related capability metric, and +128 lowers it.
claims.method: CAA at L40, Commonsense Constraint Micro Pass Rate
claims.caveat: The effect is moderate and non-monotonic. The text gives no significance test, and the authors say it is not evidence that steering generally solves planning.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: A linear probe separates short- from long-term labels on prompts checked for explicit temporal keywords.
claims.method: Logistic regression at L26, test accuracy
claims.caveat: Shuffled labels score about 50%, which rules out chance but not surface cues: no surface baseline yet. The same probe scores about 80% at layer 0.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: Probes trained on implicit pairs carry over to explicit pairs.
claims.dataset: Trained on implicit pairs, evaluated on explicit pairs
claims.method: Zero-shot transfer at L26
claims.caveat: Transfer shows the two sets share a readable contrast, not what that contrast is: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: Probes trained on explicit questions read a held-out explicit set.
claims.method: Best probe families at L28 and L32; the steering direction reaches 96.0% at L24
claims.caveat: The authors treat this as evidence the contrast is linearly accessible, not that it isolates temporal horizon: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: The same probes score lower on implicit questions.
claims.method: Explicit-trained probes, best layer per family between L24 and L32
claims.caveat: The authors say implicit examples do not fully isolate horizon: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: An unrelated variable, cumulative reliability of a reasoning chain, is also decodable in the same subgraph.
claims.method: Logistic regression in shared PCA-50 space, plateau across L19–31
claims.caveat: The direction is linearly orthogonal to temporal preference but on the same curved manifold, so the region encodes more than time.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: The steering direction may reflect a broader short-term/long-term register.
claims.method: Stated limitation on the training contrast
claims.caveat: Continuations can also vary in abstraction, urgency, strategic scope and proactive-versus-reactive framing.

claims.question: generalize
claims.claim: A direction trained on binary answers moves the indifference multiplier on a monetary task it was not trained on.
claims.dataset: Money-now versus money-later prompts, 768 generations per condition
claims.method: CAA at L40, greedy decoding, at −128, 0 and +128
claims.caveat: A random direction gives a negative-to-positive ratio of 0.39–1.69, against 4.55–14.46 for steering. L40 is an illustrative slice, and the 3650-day value is capped at the largest tested multiplier.

claims.question: generalize
claims.claim: Probe signal differs across model families.
claims.method: Linear probes compared across models
claims.caveat: Reported as a qualitative comparison. Cross-model causal patching has not been done.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: A text-only baseline matches or beats probes that appear to detect planning in generated code.
claims.dataset: Code generation samples across 5 return types
claims.method: Baseline staircase: function and parameter names against residual-stream probes
claims.caveat: Models up to 7B only. Larger models are untested.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: Refusal rates change with repetition in only some models.
claims.method: Refusal rate at repetition 1 against repetition 20
claims.caveat: Rates move in steps of 0.125, which implies few prompts per cell. Injection resistance improves with repetition in the two models tested.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: Probe activation did not precede behavioral change in the repetition study.
claims.method: Onset of probe activation against onset of behavioral change
claims.caveat: From an unpublished draft on repetition, not temporal scope. No result on this site shows a probe flagging a change in advance.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: Social pressure flips answers far more often than it produces true surrender.
claims.dataset: Sycophancy benchmarks with social pressure conditions
claims.method: Behavioral evaluation with hidden-state probes
claims.caveat: The hidden-state probe is underpowered, with 11 positive examples where about 1,000 are needed.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: Uncertainty encoding is strongest at the first reasoning step and weakens after it.
claims.method: Probes across reasoning steps
claims.caveat: Encoding varies significantly across datasets and only weakly predicts future states.

claims.question: related
claims.claim: Output entropy collapses as context fills, without a matching gain in accuracy.
claims.method: Entropy and accuracy measured across context
claims.caveat: Partly offset by in-context learning on some task patterns.

claims.question: generalize
claims.claim: An explicit-trained probe reads implicit prompts in a much smaller model.
claims.dataset: Trained on explicit pairs, evaluated on 50 implicit pairs
claims.method: Logistic regression at L10
claims.caveat: One small model and a small set: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: Earlier headline number for GPT-2.
claims.method: Cross-validation on the training set at L8
claims.caveat: A training-set score, so not evidence of generalization: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: Earlier held-out number for GPT-2.
claims.method: Cross-validated accuracy recorded within the test file at L6
claims.caveat: The file records cross-validation over its own 100 samples, not a train-to-test result: no surface baseline yet.

claims.question: really-time
claims.claim: Earlier claim of semantic encoding after keyword removal.
claims.method: Cross-validated accuracy recorded at L10–11
claims.caveat: Accuracy rises from 74–77% in the test file to 100% after keywords are removed, which needs explaining. The verification script's quick mode only prints stored values.

claims.question: steering
claims.claim: Earlier steering consistency figure for GPT-2.
claims.method: Listed as a known caveat in the results summary
claims.caveat: Specific to GPT-2, and superseded by the controlled Qwen3 sweeps above.
